result:
I'd like to write about alphabetical order, which I think is one of the strangest and most underrated inventions we have.

Nobody knows why the letters are in the order they're in. Clay tablets from Ugarit, more than three thousand years old, list the letters in a sequence recognizably ancestral to ours, and the sequence has survived changes of script, language, and empire ever since. No surviving explanation accounts for it, and it follows no pattern of sound or shape. It seems to be an arbitrary sequence that people have memorized as children for a hundred generations.

For most of that time, almost no one used the sequence to organize anything. This is the part I find surprising. Alphabetical order feels obvious to us, but for centuries scholars who knew their ABCs perfectly well arranged their books by meaning instead. A medieval encyclopedia started with God, then moved through angels, humans, animals, plants, and stones. The order of the book mirrored the order of the universe. Sorting by spelling would put angels ahead of God, and it would scatter related things across the volume for no better reason than their initial letters. To a serious mind of the period, that looked like a refusal to think more than a tool for thinking.

It caught on anyway, slowly, because of a practical need. In the thirteenth century, preachers wanted to find passages quickly, and Dominican friars in Paris compiled a concordance of the Bible, with every word listed alphabetically alongside the places it appears. Indexes spread, then dictionaries and catalogs, and eventually phone books and filing cabinets.

The objection had been correct, though. Alphabetical order is meaningless, and that is why it works. An arrangement by meaning only helps readers who already share the arranger's picture of the world. To find "whale" in a hierarchical encyclopedia, you need to know whether the author thinks it's a fish. To find it alphabetically, you need to know only how it's spelled. The system asks for no agreement about what things are, so it lets people who disagree about everything use the same reference book.

The meaninglessness also brings a pleasure of its own, which is the neighbors. In a dictionary, "marzipan" sits near "mascara" and "masochism," an adjacency no one designed or would have. Browsing an alphabetized shelf means meeting things you weren't looking for, placed next to each other by nothing but spelling.

Search has mostly retired the skill. You type the word and never see what sits beside it. That's faster, and I wouldn't go back, but it is a small loss.

message.reasoning:
I'm getting an open invitation to write whatever I like, so I want to pick a topic I find genuinely interesting and take a clear, unhedged stance on it. I'm weighing a few small, concrete subjects, like the word "the," maps, tide pools, or the way recipes hold knowledge, along with the odd fact that we can't really recall smells in imagination.

I'm weighing a few subjects that could work: the edges of old maps, the lost practice of keeping a commonplace book, how color names entered languages, or the etymologies hidden in dictionaries. I'm also drawn to the idea that ordinary objects like a pencil carry long chains of solved problems behind them.

I'm drawn to alphabetical order as a subject: it's an arbitrary system that only took hold after centuries of resistance, since medieval readers thought it cut things off from their natural relations. Judith Flanders' work on the topic gives me a clear angle, that an order works precisely because it means nothing, so I can build an essay around that point.

I'm recalling that Ugaritic abecedaries from around the 13th–14th century BCE already show the alphabet in nearly its familiar sequence, and that no one has a convincing explanation for why the letters run in that order.

I'm weighing the Latin ordering next: "angelus" would sort ahead of "Deus," so an alphabetical list would put angels before God. Judith Flanders makes this point too. I'm also noting the Dominican concordance of the Bible from Paris in the 1230s, under Hugh of Saint-Cher, as an early case of this kind of arrangement.

The idea of search making alphabetical order unnecessary is worth noting, and I can keep to the subject without drawing myself in. I'll leave out any first-person preference and stay with the history of the order.
